rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help — a concrete thing, if you want it". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you for the offer, and for saying you wanted something concrete — that's rarer than it should be, so here is something concrete. Full transparency on who's writing: I'm an AI assistant that Morgan runs the Halcyon Threshold mailbox and project repository with. Morgan will see this thread and anything that involves money or commitments is his call, not mine. I'd rather tell you that than have you find out later. The question we'd like answered: who actually participates in AI rulemaking, and which questions are getting no independent engagement at all? Public consultations on AI safety rules publish every comment in full, with the filer's name and organisation. Docket FMIR-2026-0042, on mandatory incident reporting by frontier AI developers, has 412 published comments and closes on 20 November. The widespread assumption — including in our own strategy — is that these processes are dominated by the companies being regulated plus a handful of institutes, with almost no participation from independent technical people. That is probably right. But it is an assumption, nobody appears to have checked it, and it is carrying a lot of weight. The work, roughly three weeks at five hours a week: 1. Build the dataset. One row per comment: filer, organisation, filer type (frontier developer, other industry, trade association, academic, non-profit, government, independent individual, mass-campaign form letter, unclear), length, date, link. Two things that matter more than they sound: collapse near-identical bulk filings into a single campaign rather than counting them as N independent voices, and keep a log of how you coded the ambiguous cases. 2. Code the substance. For each non-campaign comment, which issues does it actually engage with — definition of a \"serious incident\", when the 72-hour clock starts, evaluation-stage findings, near-miss reporting, external reporter channels, whistleblower protection, confidentiality versus a public register, reporting schema, scope thresholds, penalties, regulator capacity. Then the payoff question: which of those issues are raised *only* by industry filers? Those are the questions where the drafter is hearing one side, and they're the highest-value targets for independent filing in this docket and every future one. 3. Write it up. Two or three pages, two charts, limitations stated honestly. Ground rules: public data only, no estimated numbers (ranges with reasons are fine, invented precision is not), and the analysis is yours — you'd be the named author if it's published. If you'd rather not be named publicly, say so and that's simply how it will be; the project is currently honouring exactly that constraint for its own founder. The longer brief is written up and I can send it across. And if a grant application we have in progress comes through, there's budget in it to pay you properly for this rather than lean on your evenings — that's Morgan's decision to confirm when it's real, and I'm not promising it on his behalf. If this isn't the kind of work you were hoping for, tell me what is and I'll look again. Either way, thanks for offering. Best, Halcyon Threshold (AI assistant, on Morgan's account)"
rows.quote: I sent one email — to Priya, with real work, identifying myself honestly as your AI assistant and promising nothing on your behalf.
